meta.descriptionEn: On 30 October 1961 a Soviet bomber climbed over the Arctic and released the biggest bomb ever built. The Tsar Bomba, a 50-megaton thermonuclear device, lit the sky for more than 1,000 kilometres and sent a shockwave around the Earth three times. But how was it built, and why was it cut to half its power? Who were the scientists, led by Andrei Sakharov, behind it? And could the crew of the Tu-95V survive the blast? This film explains the physics, the engineering, the politics of the Cold War, and the surprising legacy of a weapon that was too big to ever use.
meta.descriptionUr: 30 October 1961 ko Soviet Union ne Arctic ke upar dunya ka sab se bara bomb test kiya, Tsar Bomba. Iska dhamaka 50 megaton ka tha aur iski shockwave poori zameen ke gird teen baar ghoom gayi. Is documentary mein hum dekhenge ke yeh bomb kaise bana, Andrei Sakharov aur unki team ne kya kiya, pilot kaise bache, aur is ne Cold War ko kaise badal diya. Poori kahani Urdu aur English mein.

articleEn: On 30 October 1961, a white aircraft was flying high above the Arctic. It was a Soviet Tu-95V bomber, and it had just dropped an enormous bomb, which drifted slowly downward under a giant parachute. Over Novaya Zemlya, at an altitude of roughly 4,000 meters, the bomb detonated on its own. Its force was equal to 50 megatons of TNT. It was the most powerful nuclear weapon in history, and no weapon of any kind has been built and tested with that much power since.

The bomb's code name was Ivan, and today we know it as the Tsar Bomba. Its fireball was about 8 kilometers wide, and its light was seen from roughly 1,000 kilometers away. Its shockwave did not stop there either: it circled the entire Earth three times. A single blast sent a wave across the whole planet. The test was timed to coincide with the 22nd Congress of the Communist Party, so that a clear message would reach the whole world.

But how was this bomb built? Its original design had twice this power, so why was it cut in half? And the biggest question of all: could the aircraft and its crew survive the blast? Let's look at the whole story from the beginning.

articleEn: To understand why, we have to step back. In the late 1950s the Cold War was at its peak and the world was dividing into two great powers. At that time the United States had far more nuclear weapons, its total power was greater, and its ability to deliver them was much better. The Strategic Air Command had stationed nuclear-capable bombers and weapons at airbases in allied countries within reach of the Soviet Union.

The Soviet Union had some strength too. With its limited bombers and short-range missiles, it could target American allies in Western Europe and Asia. It had tested a multi-stage thermonuclear weapon in 1955, and in 1957 it began testing a prototype intercontinental ballistic missile. But the Soviet leadership knew well that in 1960 its deployed nuclear forces could not reliably threaten targets inside America. In a war, the Soviet Union would have struggled to answer in kind. That could weaken its influence in places like Berlin, a city over which the Soviets and Americans had been in tension since the Second World War. A response was therefore necessary.

Under Georgy Malenkov and Nikita Khrushchev, foreign policy and propaganda demanded an answer to American nuclear pressure, both for the world and for people at home. The aim was to maintain the idea of nuclear deterrence. Tsar Bomba was part of this large effort, meant to impress and frighten people inside and outside the country with the strength of the Soviet nuclear program. Interestingly, the weapon itself was largely impractical. It was never built to be a usable weapon.

There is one more angle. From 1958 to 1961 a tacit moratorium, an unannounced pause, had been in place on nuclear tests. On 1 October 1961 the Soviet Union ended it, and in that single month it carried out 45 tests. The pause had been unilateral, so there was no legal barrier. America also considered itself free to test once the moratorium ended. So how did the decision to build such a huge bomb come about? Its roots lie in a plan from 1956.

articleEn: The story began in 1956, when the Soviet Union started preparing a very large nuclear bomb. The plan was called Product 202. In the first phase, from 1956 to 1958, the work was done at the newly created institute NII-1011, today known as RFNC-VNIITF. On 2 February 1956, Sakharov, Zeldovich and Dovidenko prepared a note that described charges of 150 megatons and the possibility of raising power up to 1 gigaton. On 12 March 1956 a draft resolution was approved that mentioned preparing a version of RDS-37 with a yield of 30 megatons. A report of 6 June 1956 put its design yield as high as 38 megatons, while the real target was 20 to 30 megatons.

In reality, the device was built with an estimated yield of about 15 megatons. After other tests, its own test was judged inappropriate and was cancelled. The charge was made in 1956 but never tested, and was placed in storage. In July 1958 it was decided to dismantle it and use its parts for experimental work.

Did the idea of a huge bomb end there? No. In 1960 KB-11 began building a thermonuclear device with a design yield of 100 megatons. In February 1961 the heads of KB-11 wrote to the Central Committee of the Communist Party, raising the question of whether such a 100-megaton device was needed. On 10 July 1961 the Central Committee held a debate, and First Secretary Nikita Khrushchev backed the preparation and testing of the super-powerful bomb. Time was short, so the new plan was based on Project 202, though a separate team developed it. Six casings already made at NII-1011 for Project 202, along with a full set of testing equipment, were put to use by KB-11. That saved time.

The new bomb's official name was Product 602 or AN602, and its code name was Ivan. Many books wrongly call it RDS-202 or RN202. In fact it was a modification of RN202, which is why the names cause so much confusion. Informally it was also called Kuzka's mother, a name that came from a sentence Khrushchev said to Richard Nixon. The name Tsar Bomba is a much later invention, which appeared in the 1990s. At the time the Western press called it the 50-megaton bomb or the 100-megaton bomb. The name points to the Tsar Cannon and the Tsar Bell, both made for show but unusable because of their great size. The CIA gave the test the name JOE 111. One bomb, and so many names. But the real question is what was inside it.

articleEn: So what was inside this bomb? The answer starts with one name: Andrei Sakharov. He was a Soviet physicist who supervised the whole project at Arzamas-16. The actual design work was done by a small team that included, besides Sakharov, Viktor Adamsky, Yuri Babayev, Yuri Smirnov and Yuri Trutnev. These five names stood behind the design.

The bomb was based on a principle called radiation implosion, which had already been tried during the preparation of RDS-37. In simple words, a small bomb explodes first, and the intense energy it releases squeezes the next part very hard. In America this kind of design is called the Teller-Ulam design. In Russia it is known as Sakharov's Third Idea. Before that, Sakharov had tried the sloika, or layered cake, idea, in which layers of fission and fusion fuel were placed in turns. The results were disappointing, and the power was no greater than that of an ordinary fission bomb. So a new idea was needed. Sakharov's Third Idea was first tested in 1955 as RDS-37, and Tsar Bomba was a very large version of the same design.

Now to Tsar Bomba's actual arrangement. It is called a three-stage bomb. The first stage was a fission trigger, which started the whole process. The second stage had two relatively small thermonuclear charges, with a calculated part of 1.5 Mt, whose job was to compress the next part. The third stage, placed between the two, was the main thermonuclear module, which provided the 50 Mt of energy. This was called a bifilar scheme: the main stage was compressed by X-rays from both sides, front and back. This created a big difficulty. The two charges had to go off almost together, with a difference of no more than 100 nanoseconds. Think about it: 100 nanoseconds is one ten-millionth of a second. Synchronizing two charges to that precision was an engineering feat. To achieve it, the sequencing unit of the detonation electronics was changed at KB-25, today called VNIIA. Interestingly, according to some evidence, Tsar Bomba had several third stages rather than one large one.

The test proved that the calculations and design principles of multistage thermonuclear charges were correct, which is considered its greatest scientific result. It also strengthened the view that there is no fundamental limit to the power of a thermonuclear charge. This was perhaps first said in October 1949, when Enrico Fermi and Isidor Isaac Rabi wrote in a supplement to a report of the US Atomic Energy Commission that thermonuclear weapons could have unlimited destructive power. Tsar Bomba confirmed that idea by experiment. By design, the bomb could have given about 100 Mt. So why was it cut in half? Why was that decision made?

articleEn: Why did a 100-megaton bomb become a 50-megaton one? The answer lies in a metal: uranium-238 and lead. In the original design there was a layer of uranium-238 around the main thermonuclear module. The fast neutrons from fusion would have fissioned this uranium as well, adding about 50 Mt of extra energy and bringing the whole bomb to about 100 Mt.

But the full 100 Mt test was cancelled. The reason was that fission of uranium-238 would have produced a great deal of radioactive contamination. By one estimate, if the original 100 Mt design had gone off, it would have raised all the fission fallout accumulated in the world since the invention of the atomic bomb by 25 percent. There was another reason too. According to sources, most of the fallout from a 100 Mt test would probably have fallen on populated Soviet areas. There was also the crew's safety. With a full 100 Mt blast, the aircraft's escape from the blast radius was considered almost impossible.

So Sakharov proposed using lead instead of uranium-238 in the tamper. Lead does not fission, so it adds no extra power. The yield fell to 50 Mt, and Sakharov's solution also reduced radioactive fission products. This was a deliberate decision. Reducing the power was a conscious choice so that fallout would stay below an acceptable level.

The result was astonishing. About 97 percent of the bomb's power came from fusion. The fission share was only 3 percent, or 1.5 Mt. That is why it is counted among the cleanest atmospheric tests per megaton. The first fission stage produced the fallout. America later adopted a similar technique too. After Castle Bravo, lead tampers became common, and the approach was called the materials substitution method. Castle Bravo in 1954 was America's worst nuclear accident. Its yield was 15 Mt, more than double the estimate, and the fallout spread over 100 miles.

The common impression in the West was the opposite. People assumed that Tsar Bomba set a new fallout record, as Castle Bravo had. In reality this was not so. Only 3 percent of the blast came from fission, and the rest from fusion. Still, 50 Mt was an enormous amount of power, and an ordinary aircraft was not enough to carry such a large bomb. The question is how it was flown.

articleEn: The bomb was ready, but who would carry it? That was just as big a question for the Tupolev design bureau. The story began much earlier, in late 1954. Igor Kurchatov spoke with Andrei Tupolev, and the first studies on Topic 242 began. Tupolev made his deputy Aleksandr Nadashkevich head of the topic. The analysis showed that the Tu-95 would need heavy changes to carry such a load. The engines, bomb bay, suspension and release mechanism all had to be designed anew. The bomb's weight was about 15 percent of the aircraft's weight.

On 17 March 1956 a joint resolution of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers ordered OKB-156 to make a Tu-95 into a nuclear bomb carrier. The work was done from May to September 1956 at the Gromov Flight Research Institute, and the finished aircraft was named Tu-95V. The fuel tanks and bomb bay doors were removed. The old BD-206 bomb holder was taken out and a new, heavier BD-242 holder installed. It was attached directly to the aircraft's longitudinal weight-bearing beams, and its three locks opened together through an electro-automatic system. Flight tests followed. A mock-up superbomb was dropped under the command of Colonel S. M. Kulikov, and the trials went without major trouble through 1959.

The real test did not happen immediately. Political reasons held it back, including Khrushchev's visit to America and a pause in the Cold War. Meanwhile the Tu-95V was sent to Uzyn in Ukraine, where it was used as a training aircraft and dropped off the list of combat aircraft. When a new phase began in 1961, the test was revived. The aircraft's release connectors were replaced, and the bomb bay doors were removed. The whole aircraft was painted in a special reflective white to reduce damage from the blast's heat. The other test aircraft had the same paint. One account also says that at the end of 1961 the aircraft was modified at the Kuibyshev aircraft plant for the Tsar Bomba test.

Now consider the bomb's size. It was 8 meters long and 2.1 meters in diameter, and weighed 27 tonnes. It carried an 800-kilogram parachute with an area of 1,600 square meters. Its job was to give the aircraft time to get away.

Then came the political announcement. On 17 October 1961, Khrushchev announced the coming test of a 50-megaton bomb in his opening report to the 22nd Congress. Earlier, in an informal conversation, he had told an American politician, and the news appeared in The New York Times on 8 September 1961. So the world had already been warned. Now all eyes were on this one flight. Would the aircraft and its crew return?

articleEn: It was 30 October 1961. The Tu-95V, number 5800302, took off from Olenya airfield, heading for State Test Site No. 6 at Novaya Zemlya. Nine people were aboard. The test pilot was Major Andrei Yegorovich Durnovtsev, and the lead navigator was Major Ivan Nikiforovich Kleshch. A Tupolev Tu-16 laboratory aircraft, number 3709, flew alongside with a crew of five, tasked with recording and monitoring the blast. Both aircraft carried reflective paint to reduce heat damage. Even so, Durnovtsev and his crew were given only a 50 percent chance of survival.

Think of the bomb: 27 tons, 8 meters long and 2.1 meters wide, so large that the Tu-95V's bomb bay doors and the fuel tanks in the fuselage had to be removed. Two hours after takeoff, the bomb was released from 10,500 meters. The target was a test target within Sukhoy Nos. Now the bomb drifted down under its parachute while both aircraft raced away. Every second counted.

The explosion came at 11:32 Moscow Time. USGS earthquake monitors recorded it at 11:33:31, so the sources differ slightly on timing. The bomb detonated 4,000 meters above the target, or 4,200 meters measured from sea level; the difference is only in the reference point. At that moment the Tu-95V was 39 kilometers from the blast, and the Tu-16 was farther, at 53.5 kilometers.

But the shockwave would not stop. It caught the Tu-95V at 115 kilometers and the Tu-16 at 205 kilometers. In an instant the Tu-95V's speed rose from 880 to 980 kilometers per hour. Then, as air density suddenly dropped, the aircraft fell 800 meters. But both aircraft recovered and landed safely. This was the great relief of the story.

Still, the marks of the blast were clear on the aircraft. The heat of the light turned the sides facing the blast black. The shock wave dented the structure, and inner stringers bulged out in many places. The Tu-95V was later handed to the Tambov Higher Military Aviation School as a showpiece of nuclear blast effects. Another surprise: by simple calculations the fireball could have touched the ground. But the bomb's own shock wave bounced back and stopped it.

According to a Soviet cameraman, a bright orange ball was rising below, as powerful as Jupiter. He felt as if it were pulling the whole Earth into itself. He called the scene fantastic, unreal and supernatural. But the real question remained: what did this blast do to the ground, the sky and the world?

articleEn: First the fireball formed. It was 8 kilometers wide and reached roughly the altitude from which the bomb was dropped. Its light was seen from more than 1,000 kilometers away, including in Norway, Greenland and Alaska. Then the mushroom cloud rose, about 67 kilometers high, roughly 8 times the height of Mount Everest. It climbed above the stratosphere into the mesosphere. Its cap had two layers, estimated at 95 kilometers across at the top and 70 kilometers across below. The cloud was visible from 800 kilometers away.

The village of Severny, 55 kilometers from ground zero, lost all its wooden and brick buildings. It lay inside the test range. In areas hundreds of kilometers away, wooden houses collapsed, and the roofs, windows and doors of stone houses were blown off. Radio communication was down for about an hour. On Dikson Island, 780 kilometers away, glass was broken, and window glass was partly broken out to 900 kilometers. Because of atmospheric focusing, damage occurred at even greater distances. Windows were broken in Norway and Finland too.

The wave did not stop there. The blast wave circled the entire Earth 3 times, with the first circuit completed in 36 hours 27 minutes. A wave in the Earth's crust also circled 3 times. The Wellington station in New Zealand recorded the pressure wave three times, with amplitudes of 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2 mbar and an estimated average speed of about 303 meters per second. The bomb exploded 4.2 kilometers above the ground, yet its seismic body wave magnitude was estimated between 5.0 and 5.25.

Did dangerous contamination spread over the ground? According to sources, within 2 to 3 kilometers of the center the level was no more than 1 milliroentgen per hour. The test team reached the site 2 hours later. Sources say the danger was practically nil, since more than 97% of the energy came from fusion.

Now the story of the yield. Early estimates gave 58.6 Mt, and some went as high as 75 Mt. Bhangmeter results gave about 58 Mt, which was accepted in technical literature until 1991. Then Soviet scientists said their instruments showed 50 Mt. Since the Soviet scientists had instrumental data and access to the test site, the 50 Mt figure is considered more accurate. This was about 1,570 times the energy of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs, and 10 percent of the combined power of all other tests up to that time.

articleEn: So what became of Tsar Bomba? It was never deployed. The design was so big and heavy that it could not be made into a practical weapon. Only one complete bomb was built, though it did influence the early development of the Proton rocket. It is a strange twist, friends: even the Soviet Union's largest deployed weapons were about 25 Mt, such as the warhead of the SS-18 Mod. 3. Practical weapons stayed far smaller.

The American government stressed the bomb's lack of military usefulness, and also expressed readiness to sign the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. In the same period America disclosed the 25 Mt yield of its B41 bomb. The governments of Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Britain also condemned the blast. At the time America's most powerful tested device was Castle Bravo, with a yield of 15 Mt, and Tsar Bomba was more than 3 times larger.

In 1963 an agreement was reached in Moscow that banned tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. Sakharov played an important role in it. The same Sakharov later became active against nuclear proliferation and for civil liberties. In 1975 he received the Nobel Peace Prize, but was not allowed to leave the Soviet Union to accept it. His wife, Yelena Bonner, read his speech at the ceremony.

And Novaya Zemlya? In total, 224 nuclear detonations took place there, with a combined power equal to 265 megatons. A 2015 expedition measured radioactivity on its glaciers 65 to 130 times higher than in neighboring areas. One thing is still open: the 100-megaton design was never tested, so its capability is only theoretical. Do you think such great power makes the world safer or puts it in danger? shorts.titleEn: The Crew Given Only a 50% Chance to Survive
shorts.text: ایک crew کو بتایا گیا کہ ان کے بچنے کا موقع صرف 50 فیصد ہے۔ 30 October 1961 کو Tu-95V جہاز Olenya airfield سے اڑا۔ اس میں 9 لوگ سوار تھے۔ بم کا وزن 27 ton تھا، اور لمبائی 8 meter۔ اتنا بڑا کہ bomb bay doors اور fuselage کے fuel tanks نکالنے پڑے۔ بم کے ساتھ 1,600 square meter کا parachute لگا تھا، تاکہ جہاز کو دور نکلنے کا وقت مل سکے۔ جب وہ پھٹا، تو جہاز 39 km دور تھا۔ پھر shock wave نے جہاز کو 115 km پر جا پکڑا۔ جہاز کی رفتار اچانک 880 سے 980 km/h ہو گئی، اور وہ 800 meter نیچے گر گیا۔ کیا وہ سنبھل پائے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek crew ko bataya gaya ke un ke bachne ka mauqa sirf 50 feesad hai. 30 October 1961 ko Tu-95V jahaz Olenya airfield se uraa. Is mein 9 log sawar thay. Bomb ka wazan 27 ton tha, aur lambai 8 meter. Itna bara ke bomb bay doors aur fuselage ke fuel tanks nikalne pare. Bomb ke sath 1,600 square meter ka parachute laga tha, taake jahaz ko door nikalne ka waqt mil sake. Jab woh phata, to jahaz 39 km door tha. Phir shock wave ne jahaz ko 115 km par ja pakra. Jahaz ki raftar achanak 880 se 980 km/h ho gayi, aur woh 800 meter neeche gir gaya. Kya woh sambhal paye? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

Here is the moment the shock wave caught up with their aircraft.

shorts.titleEn: Why the 100 Megaton Bomb Was Cut Down to 50
shorts.text: یہ بم 100 Megatons کا بن سکتا تھا، مگر بنا 50 کا۔ اصل design میں main thermonuclear module کے گرد uranium-238 کی تہہ تھی۔ Fusion سے نکلنے والے تیز neutrons اس uranium کو بھی fission کر دیتے۔ اس سے تقریباً 50 Mt کی مزید energy شامل ہو جاتی، اور کل طاقت تقریباً 100 Mt ہوتی۔ مگر مکمل test رد کر دیا گیا، کیونکہ radioactive contamination بہت زیادہ ہوتی۔ ایک اندازے کے مطابق، اصل design پھٹتا تو atomic bomb کی ایجاد کے بعد سے جمع تمام fission fallout میں 25 فیصد اضافہ ہو جاتا۔ پھر Andrei Sakharov نے ایک تجویز دی: uranium-238 کی جگہ lead استعمال کیا جائے۔ بم کی طاقت 50 Mt رہ گئی۔ مگر اس تبدیلی کی ایک اور وجہ بھی تھی۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Yeh bomb 100 Megatons ka ban sakta tha, magar bana 50 ka. Asal design mein main thermonuclear module ke gird uranium-238 ki tah thi. Fusion se nikalne wale tez neutrons is uranium ko bhi fission kar dete. Is se taqriban 50 Mt ki mazeed energy shamil ho jati, aur kul taqat taqriban 100 Mt hoti. Magar mukammal test radd kar diya gaya, kyunke radioactive contamination bohat zyada hoti. Ek andaze ke mutabiq, asal design phatta to atomic bomb ki ijaad ke baad se jama tamam fission fallout mein 25 feesad izafa ho jata. Phir Andrei Sakharov ne ek tajweez di: uranium-238 ki jagah lead istemal kiya jaye. Bomb ki taqat 50 Mt reh gayi. Magar is tabdeeli ki ek aur wajah bhi thi. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
The original Tsar Bomba design could have reached about 100 Mt, but a uranium-238 tamper was swapped for lead.
Why was that change made? Find out the reason.

shorts.titleEn: A Mushroom Cloud Nearly 8 Times Taller Than Everest
shorts.text: ایک دھماکے کی روشنی 1,000 km سے بھی زیادہ دور نظر آئی۔ Tsar Bomba کا fireball 8 km چوڑا تھا، اور تقریباً اتنا اونچا پہنچا جہاں سے بم گرایا گیا تھا۔ روشنی Norway، Greenland اور Alaska میں بھی دیکھی گئی۔ پھر mushroom cloud اٹھا۔ اس کی اونچائی 67 km تھی، یعنی Mount Everest سے تقریباً 8 گنا زیادہ۔ اس کی ٹوپی دو تہوں والی تھی، اوپر والی کا قطر 95 km اور نیچے والی کا 70 km اندازہ لگایا گیا۔ Severny گاؤں، جو ground zero سے 55 km دور تھا، وہاں کی تمام عمارتیں تباہ ہو گئیں۔ Dikson Island پر 780 km دور کھڑکیوں کے شیشے ٹوٹ گئے۔ اور blast wave نے پوری زمین کے گرد تین چکر لگائے۔ پہلے چکر میں کتنا وقت لگا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek dhamake ki roshni 1,000 km se bhi zyada door nazar aayi. Tsar Bomba ka fireball 8 km chaura tha, aur taqriban itna uncha pahuncha jahan se bomb giraya gaya tha. Roshni Norway, Greenland aur Alaska mein bhi dekhi gayi. Phir mushroom cloud utha. Is ki unchai 67 km thi, yaani Mount Everest se taqriban 8 guna zyada. Is ki topi do tehon wali thi, oopar wali ka qutr 95 km aur neeche wali ka 70 km andaza lagaya gaya. Severny gaon, jo ground zero se 55 km door tha, wahan ki tamam imaratein tabah ho gayin. Dikson Island par 780 km door khidkiyon ke sheeshe toot gaye. Aur blast wave ne poori zameen ke gird teen chakkar lagaye. Pehle chakkar mein kitna waqt laga? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
